sources.used: 模拟测试的文章、题型组合及课程计分

body.p: 雅思学术类阅读有三篇文章，共 40 题，限时 60 分钟。每种题型出几道题，各次考试不同。
本课程的模拟测试按固定的题型组合出题。双项选择题给出四组组合，选完整正确的一组。配对题从同一份选项中选择。
小测成绩是答对的比例，不换算成雅思分数段。

groups.text:
Passage 1: Comparing Shade

P1
A town study examined shade at two public squares during summer. The squares differed in layout: one had a row of mature trees along its eastern edge, while the other contained a covered walkway beside an open paved area. The study did not attempt to decide which square was more attractive. Its question was narrower: how did the areas of shade change during selected periods of the day? The team chose the two sites because both were open to the public and had clear boundaries that could be marked on a plan. A plan was drawn for each square before observations began. The plans showed paths, benches and fixed structures, but the researchers did not assume that every part of either site would be used in the same way. They also recorded the positions from which photographs could be taken without obstructing movement. These preliminary records helped the team return to comparable locations on later visits. The project was organised as a local comparison, not as a survey of every square in the town. Its findings were intended to describe the selected sites and times.

P2
On each visit, observers marked the edge of the shaded area on a copy of the appropriate plan. They used a measuring tape to locate selected points along that edge. Photographs taken from the recorded positions supplemented the plan, but the photographs did not replace the written measurements. A label on each plan identified the site and the time. Observations were made in the afternoon, with the same time intervals used at both squares. When clouds covered the sun throughout an interval, the team omitted that interval from the comparison and noted the reason. The researchers did not install permanent sensors. They brought their equipment for each visit and removed it afterwards. A notebook recorded any change to a bench or other feature that might affect the interpretation of the plans. This procedure separated a change in the position of shade from a change in the objects shown on the plan. It also allowed an incomplete observation to remain in the notebook without being treated as a full measurement. The team retained both marked plans and photographs for later checking.

P3
At the tree-lined square, the shape of the shaded area changed as the sun's position changed. The covered walkway at the second square also cast a shadow, although its outline differed from that of the trees. The observers compared the marked edges at corresponding times instead of comparing a morning observation from one site with an afternoon observation from the other. On several visits, a bench that was shaded at the beginning of an interval was exposed by the end. Staff had not moved that bench during the interval. The team treated this as an example of changing shade, not as evidence that visitors preferred either position. The report included a diagram showing the bench and the two observed edges. It also included a table listing the time of every complete observation. Entries affected by continuous cloud were recorded separately. This distinction made it possible to see which comparisons used matching observations and which intervals lacked the necessary information. The number of visitors present was not counted as part of the study, and the report made no claim about changes in attendance.

P4
The researchers concluded that a single photograph could illustrate shade at a particular moment but could not describe its movement across an afternoon. The marked plans were more useful for comparing the selected intervals because each included a time and site label. Even these records had limits. The project covered selected summer visits, not every season, and it did not establish what caused differences between years. The report gave no explanation for changes in rainfall. It recommended keeping the original plans with the summary table, so that later readers could check how a line in the table related to a marked edge. A local group subsequently used the plans to discuss where temporary seating might be placed. That discussion was separate from the study's measurements: a decision about seating would also require information about access and use. The study illustrates how a simple record can support a specific comparison when its location, timing and exclusions are visible. It also illustrates why a measurement should not be extended to questions that it was not designed to answer. The team also retained its notes on access to each observation point. Those notes helped later workers find the same position without treating a changed route as a change in the shade itself.

groups.text:
Passage 2: Publishing Bus Timetables

A town considering how to publish bus timetables faces a choice that is sometimes presented too simply. One view is that a digital display makes a printed timetable unnecessary. Another is that a printed sheet can serve every passenger on its own. I argue that neither format should be treated as a complete replacement for the other. A useful information service needs an accurate source of times and more than one way to reach it. The aim is not to make every display identical in appearance, but to let passengers obtain the same current information through a channel they can use.

Digital displays can be changed without replacing a sheet at every stop. They can also present a temporary change close to the time it takes effect. This is a substantial advantage when a route is disrupted. Yet the advantage depends on the display receiving the update. A screen that is not working or a device without a connection cannot be assumed to convey the latest information. Printed sheets have a different strength: they can be read without a powered personal device. Their limitation is that a change must be distributed and installed before the printed information is current. Both formats therefore require maintenance, although the tasks involved are different.

Three local groups have suggested priorities. The passenger access group recommends keeping printed information at stops for people who cannot rely on a personal device. The transport operators favour digital updates because they can be distributed rapidly when routes change. The local council proposes checking the date on each stop display during regular visits. These proposals address different parts of the same service: access, speed of revision and checking. They should not be treated as mutually exclusive. A printed notice can give its publication date, and a digital service can make the same date visible alongside the update. A date does not prove that a timetable is correct, but it gives a reader a way to identify which version is being viewed.

A common objection is that maintaining more than one format duplicates work. This concern deserves a response rather than dismissal. Preparing two independent sets of times would indeed create opportunities for inconsistency. A better arrangement would maintain one checked source and produce both formats from it. Staff would still have to replace sheets and monitor screens, but the times in each would originate in the same record. The extra work should be compared with the cost of leaving some passengers without accessible information. The existence of a digital option alone does not show that everyone can use it.

The distinction between a source and its displays also clarifies responsibility. A correction to a departure time should first be made in the checked source. The organisation can then publish the corrected version through the channels it maintains. If one channel is delayed, the date can help staff identify the older display. A passenger reporting a mismatch should not need to know how the internal record is stored. The report does need enough detail to identify the stop, route and version being viewed. This permits the organisation to investigate a specific discrepancy rather than assume that all copies are wrong.

There are limits to what additional formats can achieve. A timetable can communicate a scheduled departure, but it does not guarantee that a vehicle will arrive exactly on time. A temporary delay may need a separate notice, and a notice can itself become outdated. The service should therefore explain the difference between a planned schedule and a temporary update. Neither printed sheets nor screens remove the need for that distinction. A well-designed process gives staff a way to withdraw an obsolete notice as well as issue a new one. It also assigns responsibility for checking that the withdrawal has occurred.

The choice is therefore not between paper and a screen in isolation. The stronger approach combines a single checked source with formats suited to different circumstances and a method for detecting outdated displays. The passenger group's concern about access, the operators' concern about timely revision and the council's proposed checks can all contribute. More formats do not guarantee accuracy by themselves; they become useful when the information behind them is maintained. A town can evaluate the arrangement by recording reported discrepancies and checking how quickly they are corrected. Such records would assess the service actually provided rather than assume that one medium solves every problem. It can also document whether a report concerns a printed sheet or a screen. That distinction helps staff direct a correction to the appropriate display while checking the shared source.

groups.text:
Passage 3: Making a Woven Strap

A craft workshop records the stages used to make a narrow woven strap on a small hand loom. The account describes one working method, not every way a loom can be arranged. Weaving joins two sets of threads at right angles. The lengthwise threads are called the warp, while a thread passed across them is called the weft. The workshop first measures the warp threads to a consistent length. It chooses a length greater than the intended finished strap because some thread is needed to secure the ends and hold them under tension. A written record identifies the thread and the planned length before work begins. This record makes it possible to relate the finished strap to the materials selected at the start.

The warp is attached to a wooden frame. At one end, a bar holds the threads apart across the width of the strap. A second bar at the other end holds the opposite ends. The worker checks that the threads are parallel and reasonably taut. Uneven tension can make the edges difficult to keep regular. The loom also includes a heddle, a component used to separate selected warp threads from the others. When raised, it creates a gap through which the weft can pass. The heddle does not carry the weft itself. Its job is to alter the arrangement of the lengthwise threads so that a path is available.

The weft is wound onto a shuttle. The shuttle is a small carrier that can pass through the gap in the warp. After the heddle is raised, the worker moves the shuttle across and pulls enough weft through to reach the opposite edge. The heddle is then lowered and the worker changes the separation of the warp threads for the next pass. A beater is used to push the newly inserted weft towards the woven section. This places successive passes close together. The operation is repeated, with the shuttle moving across the warp and the worker checking the edges as the woven section grows.

If the weft is pulled too tightly at an edge, the strap can become narrower at that point. If it is left too loose, a loop can remain at the edge. The workshop therefore examines each edge before beating the next pass into position. When a loop is found, the worker adjusts the weft before continuing. The record distinguishes this adjustment from the act of beating: one corrects the path of the weft, while the other moves the inserted thread towards the existing fabric. The worker does not cut the warp during these intermediate checks.

When the planned woven length has been reached, the strap is removed from the frame. The ends are secured so that the woven section does not come apart. The worker then measures the finished length with a ruler and records it beside the initial planned length. The two numbers need not be identical: the first concerns the finished woven section, while the earlier measurement included extra thread for securing and tension. Treating them as measurements of the same stage would obscure that difference. The workshop retains the record with a sample of the strap.

The workshop also compares straps made with different threads, but it changes only one selected feature at a time in its teaching demonstrations. A comparison of two finished straps should state whether the thread, the planned width or another feature differed. Without that information, an observed difference cannot safely be assigned to a particular cause. Photographs can show the edges and pattern, while the written record supplies the selected materials and measurements. Neither record alone describes every stage of the process. Together they allow a later worker to trace a finished item back to the instructions and materials used to make it.

A diagram of the loom shows a frame surrounding the lengthwise warp. The heddle is positioned across those threads. A shuttle carrying the weft travels through the opening formed when the heddle is raised. The diagram represents the relation between parts rather than the whole range of hand movements. In particular, an arrow to the heddle identifies the separating component; an arrow to the shuttle identifies the carrier. The direction in which the shuttle moves is across the lengthwise warp. A reader following the description can therefore distinguish the fixed support, the threads, the separator and the carrier by their functions as well as their positions.

The process shows why the name of a component and its role should be read together. The frame supports the arrangement, the heddle separates threads, and the shuttle carries another thread through the opening. Each contributes to the formation of the fabric, but no single part performs all three functions. The example is a small-scale manual process; it does not imply that every industrial loom uses the same arrangement.

Summary: The lengthwise threads form the (1), and a thread passed across them is the (2).

Notes — preparation:
• measure the warp to a consistent (3)
• attach the warp to a wooden (4)
